newsitem.title: USA: U.S. regulators announce new car airbag rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. regulators announce new car airbag rules.

text.p: Federal regulators on Friday proposed new rules for car airbags to allow them to inflate with less explosive force and reduce the risk of injury to children and small and frail adults.

In addition to lowering the explosive force -- now up to 200 miles an hour -- the National Highway Traffic Safety Administraion said it would let owners have car dealers disconnect the airbags in their cars.

While airbags are credited with saving more than 1,100 lives in the past 10 years, they are also blamed for the deaths of at least 30 children, many of whom were riding in front seats or were unbuckled.
"Airbags are working well, but need to be improved to enhance the safety of children and small stature adults," NHTSA Administrator Ricardo Martinez said in a statement ahead of a news conference.

The force of an inflating bag can snap the neck of a child or small adult, often a woman or frail elderly person. Officials said the slower inflating airbag would continue to protect adults in most high speed crashes, yet lower the risk to children and small adults.

The NHTSA also proposed that so-called smart air bags be installed on cars beginning in the 1999 model year. These bags would sense when a child or small adult was in the passenger side seat and lower the inflation force of the bag accordingly.
